claims.text: Laser ablation of a bulk high-entropy-alloy target in a liquid can produce colloidal nanoparticles through plume cooling, condensation, and quenching.
Changing laser pulse duration and energy density modulates nanoscale cooling rates during nanoparticle formation.
Lower energy densities and shorter laser pulses limit post-nucleation atomic diffusion relative to higher-energy or longer-pulse conditions.
Limited post-nucleation diffusion kinetically traps a homogeneous, single-phase noble-metal-based high-entropy alloy.
Higher energy densities or longer pulses increase atomic mobility and cause partial phase segregation.
Rapid cooling and quenching are features of nanoparticle formation during pulsed laser ablation in liquids.
A homogeneous noble-metal-based high-entropy-alloy phase contains well-isolated active noble-metal sites.
Well-isolated noble-metal sites in the homogeneous phase produce superior catalytic performance.
Partial phase segregation diminishes catalytic performance.
Nanoparticles made with lower-energy, 100–300 fs pulses will be more compositionally uniform and more nearly single phase than particles made with higher energy and pulses approaching 1 ps.
Nanoparticles made under the lower-energy, shorter-pulse conditions will have higher catalytic activity in a benchmark reaction.
Cavitation, solvent interactions, and local thermal phenomena can influence nanoparticle formation and segregation during laser ablation in liquids.
Different nanoparticle size fractions can arise from distinct formation pathways, including condensation in a low-density mixing region and ejection from a molten target layer.
Surface segregation can depend on nanoparticle formation history, residence time in the hot mixing region, and selective oxidation.
The proposed mechanism should apply specifically to noble-metal-based high-entropy alloys synthesized by ultrafast laser ablation in colloidal environments.
Holding solvent, ambient temperature, and cavitation parameters constant while varying laser parameters provides the intended controlled comparison.
STEM, XRD, and EDX mapping will be used to assess nanoparticle morphology, phase uniformity, and elemental distribution.
Failure of the lower-energy, shorter-pulse samples to show greater phase homogeneity or superior catalytic activity would falsify the proposed hypothesis.
